subtopic_detail: Initial management of preoccupation with a perceived facial defect leading to repeated surgical consultations
stem:
A 19-year-old man is referred to your psychiatry clinic by a plastic surgeon who declined to operate on him. He has consulted two surgeons in 8 months about the shape of his nose.

He tells you he spends about 3 hours a day checking his nose in mirrors and in the reflection of his phone, and takes photographs from different angles to compare. He has stopped attending tutorials because the lighting there makes his nose look worse, and he has failed two subjects as a result.

He says his mood is flat because of how he looks, but he still enjoys gaming with friends online and his sleep and appetite are unchanged. His body mass index is 23 and he has no concerns about his weight or shape elsewhere. He accepts that others say his nose looks normal but says he can see what they cannot. There is no substance use and no suicidal ideation today. His nose appears entirely unremarkable to you.

data_table.Mental state: Preoccupied with nasal appearance, poor insight but not delusional intensity, reactive affect, no perceptual disturbance, no suicidal ideation today
data_table.History: About 3 hours daily of mirror checking and comparison photography, two surgical consultations in 8 months, two subjects failed through tutorial avoidance

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer him back to the plastic surgeon for a third opinion about corrective rhinoplasty
options.rationale: Cosmetic surgery in this setting usually leaves the preoccupation unchanged or transfers it to another body part, and dissatisfaction after operating is the rule rather than the exception. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body dysmorphic disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body dysmorphic disorder

options.text: Start olanzapine at a low nightly dose to address the fixity of his appearance beliefs
options.rationale: Antipsychotic monotherapy is not effective for body dysmorphic disorder even when insight is poor, and the poor insight specifier does not convert the condition into a psychotic illness. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body dysmorphic disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body dysmorphic disorder

options.text: Start diazepam for the distress and review him again in the clinic in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines carry dependence risk in a young adult and treat only the surface distress, while allowing the avoidance and checking cycle that maintains the disorder to continue. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy that includes exposure and response prevention
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy tailored to body dysmorphic disorder, targeting mirror checking, comparison and avoidance through exposure and response prevention, is first line treatment and works even where insight is poor. A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is added where symptoms are severe or therapy alone is insufficient, typically at doses higher than those used for depression. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body dysmorphic disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body dysmorphic disorder
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Start sertraline at a standard antidepressant dose and review him again in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors do help, but body dysmorphic disorder typically needs doses at the upper end of the range and a longer trial of 12 weeks, and medication alone is a weaker starting point than therapy. The distinguishing point from depression treatment is the dose and duration required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Body dysmorphic disorder is a preoccupation with one or more perceived defects in appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others, accompanied by repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, grooming, comparing or seeking reassurance. It sits in the obsessive compulsive and related disorders group rather than with the psychotic disorders, and around a third of patients hold their beliefs with delusional conviction without that changing the treatment. Prevalence is far higher in cosmetic surgery and dermatology clinics than in the general population, and outcomes after cosmetic procedures are poor. Suicidal ideation and attempts are common and should be asked about directly at every review. Treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for the disorder, with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at higher than usual doses for more severe presentations.
key_points: Classified with obsessive compulsive and related disorders, not with psychotic illness, even when insight is absent
Cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention is first line treatment
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors need higher doses and a 12-week trial compared with depression
Cosmetic procedures rarely help and commonly shift the preoccupation elsewhere
Screen actively for suicidal ideation, which is frequent in this disorder
explanation.pearls: Muscle dysmorphia is the body dysmorphic disorder variant seen mostly in young men who believe they are insufficiently muscular, and it should prompt direct questioning about anabolic steroid use.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body dysmorphic disorder

subtopic_detail: Management of accumulated possessions creating a fire risk in an older person with intact cognition
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community older persons mental health team. A 72-year-old widow is referred after the fire brigade attended her home for a smoke alarm and reported that they could not reach the kitchen.

She lives alone in the house she has owned for 40 years. The team's home visit found narrow walking paths between stacks of newspapers and shopping bags reaching shoulder height, a stove that cannot be used and a bath filled with boxes. She sleeps in an armchair because the bed is covered.

She tells you calmly that everything there may be useful one day and becomes visibly distressed when you raise discarding anything. She keeps no animals. She is fully orientated, her Montreal Cognitive Assessment score is 28 out of 30 with no functional decline reported outside the home, and she manages her own finances and medications accurately. There are no delusions, no hallucinations and no pervasive low mood. Her daughter has offered to organise a skip bin and clear the house next weekend.

data_table.Mental state: Calm, orientated, distressed at the prospect of discarding, no delusions or hallucinations, no pervasive low mood
data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 28 out of 30, manages finances and medications accurately
data_table.Home visit: Narrow walking paths, stacks to shoulder height, stove and bath unusable, sleeping in an armchair

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange an aged care assessment with a view to residential placement for her safety
options.rationale: She has intact cognition, manages her own affairs and has expressed no wish to move, so placement would be a disproportionate response that overrides her autonomy rather than treating a treatable disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder

options.text: Refer for hoarding specific cognitive behavioural therapy with a home based component
options.rationale: Hoarding disorder responds best to a cognitive behavioural approach that addresses beliefs about possessions, decision making and sorting skills, and that is delivered at least partly in the home where the behaviour occurs. Engagement is the central therapeutic task, and it is destroyed by imposed clearance, so building the working alliance first is what makes subsequent risk reduction possible. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Support the daughter's plan for a full house clearance by a commercial team next weekend
options.rationale: Forced clearance produces severe distress, frequently ruptures family relationships and is followed by re-accumulation within months because the underlying beliefs and decision making difficulties are untouched. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder

options.text: Start sertraline as monotherapy and review her symptoms in the clinic in 8 weeks
options.rationale: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors have modest evidence in hoarding disorder and are used where depression or obsessive compulsive disorder coexists, neither of which is present here; medication alone is not the treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Apply to the guardianship tribunal for a financial and accommodation management order
options.rationale: Guardianship requires impaired decision making capacity, and she demonstrates intact cognition and competent management of her affairs; disagreeing with her choices is not the legal test. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder

explanation.summary: Hoarding disorder is a distinct diagnosis characterised by persistent difficulty discarding possessions because of a perceived need to save them, with accumulation that congests living areas and compromises their intended use. It must be separated from the accumulation seen in obsessive compulsive disorder, where saving is driven by contamination or harm obsessions, and from the neglect of squalor associated with frontal dementia, psychosis or severe depression, which is why cognitive screening and mental state examination matter at the outset. Insight is often poor and referral usually comes from a third party such as a family member, council or fire service rather than the person. Risk to the individual and to neighbours, from fire, falls and structural load, requires a coordinated response involving housing, council and fire services alongside clinical care. Forced clearance is the single most common and most counterproductive intervention, so a harm reduction approach with graded, negotiated clearance is preferred.
key_points: Hoarding disorder is a distinct diagnosis and is not simply a form of obsessive compulsive disorder
Exclude dementia, psychosis and severe depression with cognitive testing and mental state examination
Cognitive behavioural therapy with a home based sorting component is the treatment with the best evidence
Forced clearance causes distress, ruptures relationships and is followed by re-accumulation
Coordinate with council, housing and fire services for risk reduction while therapy proceeds
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the stove, bath, bed and exits are usable; loss of function of these four is a better measure of severity and risk than any estimate of how much has been accumulated.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological adjunct for a body focused repetitive behaviour causing skin damage
stem:
A 24-year-old woman is referred to your psychiatry clinic by her general practitioner because of open sores on both forearms that have been swabbed twice and treated with antibiotics without lasting improvement.

She tells you she picks at small bumps on her arms while watching television in the evening and sometimes while sitting in meetings, and that she often realises she has been doing it only when she sees blood. She has tried wearing long sleeves and keeping her nails short. She spends about an hour a day on it and has stopped wearing short sleeves to work.

She describes the picking as a way of smoothing the skin rather than as a response to any thought about contamination or harm. She is not distressed about her general appearance and has no preoccupation with any specific body part. She denies suicidal intent and says the lesions are not made to hurt herself. Her mood is reactive, her sleep is unchanged and she uses no substances. Examination shows excoriations at varying stages of healing on the extensor forearms with no cellulitis.

data_table.Examination: Excoriations at varying stages of healing on both extensor forearms, no surrounding cellulitis or lymphangitis
data_table.Mental state: Reactive affect, no preoccupation with appearance, no contamination or harm obsessions, no suicidal intent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to dermatology for patch testing and a further course of topical antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: The lesions are self-induced, so dermatological treatment addresses the consequence rather than the behaviour and repeats the cycle that two antibiotic courses have already failed to break. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body focused repetitive behaviours)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body focused repetitive behaviours

options.text: Start olanzapine at a low nightly dose and review the lesions again in 8 weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not indicated for a body focused repetitive behaviour in the absence of psychosis or delusional infestation, and the metabolic burden is unjustified here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Advise a dialectical behaviour therapy programme for what is functioning as deliberate self-harm
options.rationale: Excoriation disorder is not deliberate self-harm; she describes an automatic grooming behaviour with no intent to injure and no affect regulation function, which is the distinction that determines which therapy is offered. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body focused repetitive behaviours)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body focused repetitive behaviours

options.text: Start diazepam to be taken in the evening when the urge to pick is at its strongest
options.rationale: As-required benzodiazepines reinforce the urge-relief cycle, carry dependence risk and have no evidence base in body focused repetitive behaviours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Start N-acetylcysteine 1200 mg twice daily alongside referral for habit reversal training
options.rationale: Habit reversal training is the psychological treatment of choice for excoriation disorder, and N-acetylcysteine at around 1200 to 2400 mg daily is the pharmacological adjunct with the best randomised evidence, thought to act through glutamate modulation in the corticostriatal circuits. The picking she describes is automatic and grooming-driven rather than obsessional, which is what places it in this group rather than with obsessive compulsive disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body focused repetitive behaviours)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body focused repetitive behaviours
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Excoriation disorder and trichotillomania are the two body focused repetitive behaviours listed within the obsessive compulsive and related disorders, and both are commonly missed because patients present to dermatology rather than to mental health services. The behaviour is usually automatic and grooming-like, often occurring during sedentary activities, and it is distinguished from obsessive compulsive disorder by the absence of any preceding obsession, from body dysmorphic disorder by the absence of appearance preoccupation, and from deliberate self-harm by the absence of intent to injure. Habit reversal training, which pairs awareness training with a competing response, is the psychological treatment with the strongest support. N-acetylcysteine has replicated randomised evidence in trichotillomania and supportive evidence in excoriation disorder, and its favourable side effect profile makes it a reasonable adjunct. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are used where a mood or anxiety disorder coexists, with weaker direct evidence for the picking itself.
key_points: Automatic grooming-driven picking with no preceding obsession and no intent to injure defines excoriation disorder
Habit reversal training is the first line psychological treatment
N-acetylcysteine around 1200 to 2400 mg daily is the adjunct with the best randomised evidence
Distinguish it from obsessive compulsive disorder, body dysmorphic disorder and deliberate self-harm, which lead to different treatments
Repeated antibiotic courses for the lesions treat the consequence, not the behaviour
explanation.pearls: N-acetylcysteine typically needs 8 to 12 weeks before benefit appears, so patients stopping at 4 weeks because nothing has changed is the commonest reason an adequate trial is never completed.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body focused repetitive behaviours

subtopic_detail: Choosing smoking cessation pharmacotherapy for a person with stable schizophrenia
stem:
A 41-year-old man attends your community mental health clinic for his monthly review. He has schizophrenia, has been stable for 3 years on paliperidone palmitate depot, and works part time in a warehouse.

He has smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 20 years and tells you he now wants to stop because his father has just been diagnosed with lung cancer. He has tried nicotine patches twice, each time lasting about 3 weeks before relapsing, and says the cravings in the first hour of the morning defeated him both times.

He is not taking clozapine and has no other regular medications. He has had no admission for 3 years, has no current depressive symptoms, no suicidal thoughts and no history of suicide attempts. He drinks alcohol rarely and uses no other substances. His weight and metabolic screen are stable and his renal function is normal.

data_table.Mental state: Euthymic, no psychotic symptoms, no suicidal ideation, insight preserved
data_table.Medications: Paliperidone palmitate depot monthly, no other regular medications
data_table.History: 25 cigarettes daily for 20 years, two failed attempts with nicotine patch monotherapy, no admission for 3 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Nicotine patch monotherapy again, with a higher strength patch and a longer planned course
options.rationale: Patch alone has already failed twice and does not address the intense morning cravings that defeated him; if nicotine replacement is used it should be combined patch plus an oral form for breakthrough craving. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation

options.text: Bupropion with a planned quit date 2 weeks after starting, and review at 4 weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion is an effective option, but it is less effective than varenicline in head to head trials and lowers the seizure threshold, so it is generally the second choice when varenicline is available and tolerated. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation

options.text: Varenicline with a planned quit date and mental state review at 2 and 4 weeks
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective single agent for smoking cessation, and the large randomised safety trial in people with and without psychiatric illness found no excess of neuropsychiatric adverse events attributable to it, which removed the historical objection to its use in schizophrenia. Scheduled mental state review remains sensible practice in a person with a psychotic illness making a major behavioural change. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Nortriptyline started at a low dose and titrated, with a quit date at 3 weeks
options.rationale: Nortriptyline has modest evidence in smoking cessation but is unsubsidised for this purpose, has anticholinergic and cardiac effects, and sits well down the Australian treatment ladder. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation

options.text: Behavioural support alone, avoiding pharmacotherapy because of his psychiatric diagnosis
options.rationale: Withholding effective pharmacotherapy from people with severe mental illness is the anti-pattern responsible for much of the roughly 15 to 20 year life expectancy gap in this population, and behavioural support alone has far lower quit rates. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on physical health of people with mental illness)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on physical health of people with mental illness

explanation.summary: Smoking rates among Australians with schizophrenia remain around two to three times the general population rate, and tobacco-related disease is a major contributor to the life expectancy gap in severe mental illness. Clinicians historically avoided varenicline in this group after post-marketing reports of neuropsychiatric events, but a large randomised trial comparing varenicline, bupropion, nicotine patch and placebo in cohorts with and without psychiatric disorders found no significant excess of neuropsychiatric adverse events, and regulatory boxed warnings were subsequently removed. Combination nicotine replacement, meaning a patch for background craving plus an oral form for breakthrough, is the alternative where varenicline is unsuitable. Behavioural support roughly doubles the effect of any pharmacotherapy and should always accompany it. One pharmacokinetic point is essential to remember: tobacco smoke induces cytochrome P450 1A2, so stopping smoking raises clozapine and olanzapine concentrations substantially and requires dose review and monitoring.
key_points: Varenicline is the most effective single agent and is not contraindicated in schizophrenia
Combination nicotine replacement, patch plus an oral form, outperforms patch alone
Behavioural support should accompany every pharmacological attempt
Withholding cessation therapy from people with severe mental illness widens the life expectancy gap
Smoking cessation raises clozapine and olanzapine levels through loss of cytochrome P450 1A2 induction
explanation.pearls: Clozapine plasma concentrations can rise by 50 to 100 per cent within 2 to 4 weeks of stopping smoking, so reduce the dose proactively and check a level when a clozapine-treated patient quits.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation
RANZCP: Position statement on physical health of people with mental illness

subtopic_detail: Interpreting hypercalcaemia with a non suppressed parathyroid hormone during long term lithium therapy
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community mental health clinic. A 58-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder attends for routine monitoring. She has taken lithium for 12 years and has had no admission in that time.

She mentions in passing that she has become constipated over the past 6 months and drinks more water than she used to. She has no bone pain, no renal colic and no recent fractures. Her weight is stable and she has no night sweats.

Her lithium level taken 12 hours post dose is 0.7 mmol/L. Her corrected calcium is 2.78 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), phosphate is 0.68 mmol/L (0.75-1.50) and parathyroid hormone is 9.8 pmol/L (1.6-6.9). Creatinine is 88 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 68 mL/min/1.73m2, thyroid stimulating hormone is 2.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 74 nmol/L (above 50) and serum protein electrophoresis shows no paraprotein. She has no tremor, no ataxia and no confusion.

data_table.Examination: No tremor, no ataxia, no confusion, no bone tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L at 12 hours post dose, corrected calcium 2.78 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), phosphate 0.68 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), parathyroid hormone 9.8 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), creatinine 88 micromol/L with estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL/min/1.73m2, thyroid stimulating hormone 2.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 74 nmol/L (above 50), serum protein electrophoresis with no paraprotein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop the lithium today and start sodium valproate as a replacement mood stabiliser
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium cessation carries a well described rebound risk of mania and of suicide, and the hypercalcaemia here is mild and asymptomatic apart from constipation, so the decision to change agents belongs to a planned discussion weighing endocrine against psychiatric risk. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Start intravenous sodium chloride 0.9 per cent and give zoledronic acid for the hypercalcaemia
options.rationale: Acute hypercalcaemia treatment is reserved for levels above about 3.0 mmol/L or for symptomatic patients with confusion, vomiting or dehydration, and bisphosphonates do not address a parathyroid-driven process. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Request a skeletal survey and urine electrophoresis to investigate for multiple myeloma
options.rationale: Myeloma causes hypercalcaemia by bone resorption independent of the parathyroid, so the parathyroid hormone would be suppressed rather than raised, and the serum electrophoresis is already clear. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Withhold the next two lithium doses and repeat the level in 48 hours for presumed toxicity
options.rationale: Her level of 0.7 mmol/L is squarely therapeutic and she has none of the neurological features of toxicity; the abnormality is calcium metabolism, not lithium concentration. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Continue the lithium and refer for endocrine assessment of the raised parathyroid hormone
options.rationale: Hypercalcaemia with a parathyroid hormone that is not suppressed is parathyroid-driven, and long term lithium causes exactly this picture by raising the calcium set point at which parathyroid hormone secretion is inhibited. Endocrine assessment decides between observation, parathyroid surgery and a change of mood stabiliser, which is a decision that should be made with the psychiatric risk of stopping lithium explicitly weighed. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders
Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

explanation.summary: Long term lithium therapy requires monitoring of renal function, thyroid function and calcium, and the calcium arm is the one most often forgotten. Lithium reduces the sensitivity of the calcium sensing receptor on parathyroid cells, so a higher serum calcium is needed before parathyroid hormone secretion is suppressed, producing a biochemical picture indistinguishable from primary hyperparathyroidism. The first interpretive step in any hypercalcaemia is the parathyroid hormone: if it is raised or inappropriately normal, the process is parathyroid-driven, whereas malignancy, myeloma, sarcoidosis and vitamin D excess all suppress it. Lithium-associated hyperparathyroidism differs from sporadic primary hyperparathyroidism in being more often multiglandular, which affects the surgical approach. Stopping lithium does not reliably reverse the abnormality once it is established, which is one reason the decision to change mood stabiliser is not automatic.
key_points: Check calcium alongside renal and thyroid function at least annually during lithium therapy
A raised or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone with hypercalcaemia means a parathyroid-driven process
Malignancy, myeloma, sarcoidosis and vitamin D excess all suppress parathyroid hormone
Lithium raises the calcium set point of the calcium sensing receptor, mimicking primary hyperparathyroidism
Do not stop lithium reflexively; rebound mania and suicide risk must be weighed against mild hypercalcaemia
explanation.pearls: Lithium-associated hyperparathyroidism is frequently multiglandular rather than a single adenoma, so localisation imaging can be negative and the surgeon may need to explore all four glands.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders
